Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Fourteen months ago, Nneka was walking from her cruiser to a corner convenience store when a man vaulted from behind a dumpster and pinned her against the wet asphalt. He didn’t just grab her; he crushed her ribs under his weight, his breath hot and reeking of stale liquor, while he told her she would never be a real officer again. The struggle was frantic, the cold pavement biting into her palms, but when she finally broke free and the assailant fled into the alley, the middle forty minutes simply vanished. She could not recall the sounds of the struggle, the exact words he whispered, or the precise moment he stopped. The blankness in her mind was absolute, leaving only a hollow, terrifying silence where her body had been fighting for survival. When those fragmented blanks began to surface during her off-hours, they dragged a visceral, bruising pain directly into her shoulders and ribs, the exact same physical ache she had felt against the ground. Each time the pain returned, it was immediately followed by a white-hot rage that tightened her throat and made her hands tremble. Because the memory refused to form a coherent whole, Nneka started filling the gaps with a quiet, punishing logic. She told herself that any other woman would have dodged the attack, would have fought back like her training dictated, or would have simply never walked alone that night. That belief took root and hardened into a conviction that she had permanently changed for the worse, fundamentally altered at her core. The realization pushed her away from her parish women’s fellowship, where she had found cultural grounding for decades, and she stopped attending, convinced that her fractured silence would only burden the community she no longer felt part of. This unshakable sense of permanent damage, layered with the belief that her own choices had irrevocably broken her, forced Nneka into a rigid perimeter of emotional avoidance. She could no longer tolerate situations that made her feel strong emotions; precinct morning debriefs, once a routine of shared banter, now felt like a minefield. When dispatch crackled with loud, aggressive tones over the radio, or when a partner raised their voice during a shift handoff, Nneka’s breath would catch and she’d quietly excuse herself to the stairwell. To keep the internal tide at bay, she started steering clear of any disagreement or confrontation, even with her husband, Marcus. When he tried to ask about her day, she would deflect, change the subject, or sit in silence, terrified that inviting tension would crack the dam. Instead of processing, she engaged in quiet counterfactual thinking during her long drives to the station, endlessly replaying a perfect alternate timeline where she had taken a different route, where she never felt the gravel cut her hands, where she remained the woman she was before the asphalt. The physical pain and sudden fury that hijacked her whenever a memory surfaced directly fuelled these avoidance habits, turning them into a daily survival rhythm. During a domestic dispute call last month, when the husband’s voice escalated and mirrored the assailant’s earlier threats, Nneka froze in her seat, her training short-circuiting against the wave of physiological dread. She radioed for backup without stepping out of her cruiser, watching the situation unfold through her window while her shoulders ached with phantom bruising. The incident wasn’t formally reported, but Marcus found her sitting in the parked car long after the call ended, staring at her hands. He told her he missed her, that her silence felt like a wall, but she couldn’t explain that opening the door to his questions would mean opening the door to the pain she couldn’t outrun. What finally brought Nneka to the clinic was the morning her sergeant placed her pending review on her desk, the quiet resignation in his voice mirroring her own fear that she was permanently damaged. She came to the intake room hoping for a way to quiet the rage without losing herself, terrified that the only path forward meant accepting the life she had been living, but secretly desperate to remember what it felt like to be safe in her own body.
